An Autumn Escape to Mt Oeta’s Quieter Side

By Lida Katsanouli | October 2nd, 2026
Greece IsMainlandExperience

A visit to a historic spa town, where legends of witches and walks through the forest reveal a lesser-known side of the mountain.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:56
Instaread

After a drive of about two and a half hours from Athens, we reached the foothills of Mt Oeta, which rises above the Spercheios Valley. Also known as the “Mountain of Hercules,” Oeta, with its dense fir and oak forests, is an inviting place for an autumn escape into nature.

1. Starting in Loutra Ypatis

From the plain of Lamia, we crossed the Spercheios River and arrived in Loutra Ypatis, a village with well-maintained parks and plenty of guesthouses. The first building we saw was the imposing Oeta Hotel, built in 1896. It carried our imaginations back to a time when visitors arrived at the spa town by carriage for restful, restorative holidays.

Passing the hydrotherapy center, I saw people of all ages enjoying the outdoor pool, which stays open until the end of October. A little farther on, Café Argo, a wood-paneled café-bar with a pool table, reminded me of an American saloon. I made a mental note to return on a cold winter evening after a day exploring the mountain.

This side of Oeta around Ypati sees fewer tourists than the area around the village of Pavliani, and yet the history of Ypati, the ancient capital of the Aenianians, should make it a compelling destination in its own right.

2. Exploring Ypati

At the Byzantine Museum of Phthiotis, which opened in 2007, we explored the history of the wider region from the early Christian period to the late Byzantine era.

A little farther on, the Kakogiannio Observatory of Ypati offers a different kind of journey through the study of the night sky. Visits can be arranged with the Phthiotis Amateur Astronomers’ Association.

Scattered ruins are all that remain of the ancient city. At Ypati Castle, surviving structures include the remains of a circular tower whose exact date is uncertain. To reach it, we followed a circular hiking route of less than 5 km, part of which can also be covered by 4×4 vehicles.

3. The Trail of the Witches

Another hiking option, the moderately challenging Trail of the Witches, is an excellent introduction to Mt Oeta. Its Greek name, Farmakides, refers to the legendary witches of Ypati who, according to tradition, made love potions from local herbs. The route passes Kremastos Waterfall, where water plunges from a height of about 45 meters. The final section has more demanding passages, so check the trail’s condition before setting out.

For experienced hikers, routes continue higher up the mountain toward the Hellenic Mountaineering Club of Lamia’s mountain hut. It can be reached on foot from Ypati (an 8-9 km hike with nearly 1,400 meters of elevation gain) or by 4×4 vehicle. From there, the Livadies Plateau in Mt Oeta National Park provides access to the high peaks of Greveno and Pyrgos.

4. A Walk and a Meal in Lychno

From Ypati, we drove up the winding road, passing first through Kapnochori, where a decommissioned military aircraft stands as a monument near the Chapel of Profitis Ilias, before reaching the village of Lychno.

Before sitting down to enjoy mutton and souvlaki beneath a plane tree at the Skandalos brothers’ taverna, Koutouki tou Lychnou, we took an easy 2.5 km circular walk through the forest. On the Charavgia Trail, we felt as though we had entered a fairyland. Small bridges spanning running water and light-hearted messages on signs along the way, all erected by the local cultural association, heightened the feeling. The route would be just as lovely for a stroll after lunch.

As so often happens in the mountains, the weather changed suddenly. Our outing on Oeta ended with a complimentary serving of halva at the taverna and a light drizzle that soon turned into a downpour. We set off back toward Ypati; autumn had made its presence felt.
